Cloud Computing.explanation: Cloud computing delivers computing resources over the internet on demand at any scale
points: Eliminates upfront capital expense for hardware and enables pay-as-you-go pricing
Provides elasticity — scale from zero to thousands of instances in minutes
Three main service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS cover different levels of management
Global infrastructure with regions and availability zones ensures low latency and high availability
Foundation for modern AI/ML workloads, big data, containers, and serverless applications

AWS.explanation: Amazon Web Services is the world's largest cloud platform with over 200 services
points: Pioneered public cloud in 2006 and still holds largest market share
Most comprehensive service catalog including compute, storage, databases, AI/ML, IoT
Global infrastructure with 30+ geographic regions and 100+ Availability Zones
Dominates enterprise adoption due to maturity, reliability and extensive partner ecosystem
Revenue engine of Amazon — consistently high-margin and fast-growing

Google Cloud.explanation: Google Cloud Platform offers cloud services powered by Google's global infrastructure
points: Built on same infrastructure that runs Google Search, YouTube, Gmail, Maps
Excels in data analytics (BigQuery), Kubernetes (GKE), and AI/ML capabilities
Strongest networking performance and lowest egress fees among major providers
Rapidly gaining enterprise traction with Anthos multi-cloud/hybrid platform
Focus on open-source contributions (Kubernetes, Istio, TensorFlow)

Microsoft Azure.explanation: Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform tightly integrated with enterprise Windows products
points: Deep integration with Active Directory, Office 365, Power BI, Dynamics 365
Strong hybrid cloud story with Azure Arc and Azure Stack
Fastest-growing major cloud provider in recent years
Leading in Windows Server, SQL Server, .NET workloads in the cloud
Significant government and regulated industry adoption

Serverless.explanation: Serverless lets you run code without managing servers — you pay only per execution
points: Automatic scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent executions
Pay-per-request pricing model eliminates idle capacity costs
Event-driven architecture perfect for microservices and API backends
Cold start latency remains primary performance consideration
Enables developers to focus purely on business logic instead of infrastructure

AWS Lambda.explanation: Lambda is AWS's serverless compute service that runs code in response to events
points: Supports many languages including Node.js, Python, Java, Go, .NET, Rust
Triggers from 200+ AWS services plus custom events via EventBridge
15-minute maximum execution time and 10 GB memory limit (2025)
Provisioned concurrency eliminates cold starts for latency-sensitive workloads
Powers massive portions of Alexa, iRobot, Coca-Cola vending machines, etc.

S3.explanation: AWS S3 is virtually unlimited object storage for files, images, backups, and data lakes
points: 11 nines (99.999999999%) durability for standard storage class
Multiple storage classes (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier) for cost optimization
Event notifications, replication, versioning, object lock for compliance
Powers static websites, big data lakes, backups, media serving worldwide
S3 Select and Athena enable querying data in-place without moving it

EC2.explanation: AWS EC2 provides resizable virtual machines in the cloud for any workload
points: Instance types optimized for compute, memory, storage, GPU, HPC, etc.
Spot Instances up to 90% discount for fault-tolerant workloads
Bare metal instances for direct hardware access
Graviton processors (Arm-based) offer better price/performance
Still the foundational compute primitive for most serious AWS deployments

VPC.explanation: A Virtual Private Cloud is your own isolated network section within a public cloud
points: Complete control over IP addressing, subnets, route tables, gateways
Security groups (stateful firewall) and network ACLs (stateless)
Private connectivity options: VPN, Direct Connect, PrivateLink
Flow Logs for network monitoring and forensics
Foundation for secure, multi-tier application architectures

IAM.explanation: Identity and Access Management controls who can do what across all your cloud resources
points: Least privilege principle is core design philosophy
Roles, policies, groups, users, temporary credentials via STS
Identity federation with SAML, OIDC, AWS SSO
IAM Access Analyzer finds unused permissions and external access
Fine-grained resource-level permissions for most services

CDN.explanation: A Content Delivery Network caches content at edge locations worldwide for fast delivery
points: Reduces latency by serving content from location closest to user
Handles traffic spikes without overloading origin servers
Improves security with DDoS mitigation and WAF integration
Caches both static assets and dynamic content with edge computing
Critical for global applications, video streaming, gaming, APIs

CloudFront.explanation: AWS CloudFront is a global CDN that speeds up delivery of websites, APIs, and media
points: 200+ edge locations worldwide for extremely low latency
Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions for edge compute
Field-level encryption and HTTPS enforcement
Real-time metrics and logging integration with CloudWatch
Free tier includes 1 TB/month data transfer (2025)

Auto Scaling.explanation: Auto scaling automatically adds or removes compute instances based on demand
points: Target tracking, step scaling, scheduled scaling policies
Works with EC2, ECS, DynamoDB, Aurora, Lambda (provisioned concurrency)
Predictive scaling uses ML to anticipate load patterns
Instance refresh for rolling updates with zero downtime
Critical for cost optimization and handling unpredictable traffic

Elastic Load Balancing.explanation: ELB distributes incoming traffic across multiple healthy EC2 instances automatically
points: Three types: Application Load Balancer (HTTP/HTTPS), Network Load Balancer (TCP/UDP), Gateway Load Balancer
ALB supports path-based routing, host-based routing, WebSockets
Health checks automatically remove unhealthy targets
Sticky sessions, SSL termination, connection draining
Integrated with Auto Scaling groups for dynamic scaling

RDS.explanation: AWS RDS is a managed relational database service supporting MySQL, Postgres, and more
points: Automates backups, patching, replication, failover
Multi-AZ deployment for high availability
Read replicas for horizontal scaling of reads
Performance Insights for query optimization
Supported engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server

Aurora.explanation: Aurora is AWS's cloud-native database offering up to 5x MySQL performance
points: MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible
Separates compute from storage — scales storage automatically
15 read replicas, global databases for cross-region replication
Serverless option with auto-pause and pay-per-second billing
Up to 90% cost reduction compared to commercial databases

DynamoDB.explanation: DynamoDB is AWS's serverless NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond response times
points: Fully managed, scales throughput and storage automatically
On-demand capacity mode eliminates provisioning
Global tables for multi-region replication
DAX in-memory cache for microsecond latency
Used by Alexa, iRobot, Duolingo, Lyft at massive scale

ElastiCache.explanation: ElastiCache provides managed Redis and Memcached caching in the cloud
points: Fully managed Redis (clustered/non-clustered) and Memcached
Multi-AZ with automatic failover for Redis
Online cluster resizing and engine upgrades
Used for session stores, leaderboards, real-time analytics
Redis 7 support with new data structures and functions

SQS.explanation: AWS SQS is a managed message queue for decoupling distributed application components
points: Standard queue (high throughput) vs FIFO queue (exactly-once + ordering)
At-least-once delivery with visibility timeout
Dead-letter queues for failed messages
Used for workload buffering, task queuing, fan-out patterns
Scales transparently to millions of messages per second

SNS.explanation: AWS SNS is a pub-sub messaging service for fan-out notifications to many subscribers
points: Supports push notifications to mobile, SMS, email, Lambda, SQS, HTTP
Message filtering at subscriber level
FIFO topics for ordered delivery
Used for alerts, fan-out, mobile push, workflow orchestration
High durability with multiple retries

EventBridge.explanation: EventBridge is a serverless event bus connecting AWS services and SaaS apps with routing rules
points: Schema registry and schema discovery
Event pattern matching and content-based routing
SaaS integrations (Shopify, Datadog, PagerDuty, etc.)
Archive and replay capabilities
Successor to CloudWatch Events with much more power

Kinesis.explanation: AWS Kinesis processes real-time streaming data from millions of sources simultaneously
points: Kinesis Data Streams for custom processing
Kinesis Data Firehose for easy loading to S3/Redshift
Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL processing of streams
Kinesis Video Streams for video ingestion
Used by Netflix, Hulu, Adobe, many IoT applications

ECS.explanation: AWS ECS is a managed container orchestration service for running Docker containers
points: Two launch types: EC2 and Fargate (serverless)
Tight integration with other AWS services
Task definitions and services for long-running workloads
AWS Copilot CLI simplifies deployment
Large enterprise deployments still common despite Kubernetes growth

EKS.explanation: AWS EKS is a managed Kubernetes service removing the burden of running control planes
points: Certified Kubernetes conformant
Fargate and EC2 worker node options
AWS-managed control plane with automatic upgrades
Tight integration with IAM, VPC, CloudWatch
Popular for teams already invested in Kubernetes

Fargate.explanation: AWS Fargate runs containers without managing any underlying servers or clusters
points: Serverless compute for ECS and EKS
Pay only for vCPU and memory used by containers
No need to provision or manage EC2 instances
Improved security with isolated kernel per task
Increasingly preferred for new container deployments

App Runner.explanation: AWS App Runner deploys containerized web apps automatically from code or images
points: Fully managed service — no infrastructure to configure
Supports source code from GitHub or container images
Automatic scaling, load balancing, SSL
Built-in CI/CD from container registry or Git
Simplest way to run web applications on AWS

API Gateway AWS.explanation: AWS API Gateway creates, manages, and secures REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at scale
points: Multiple API types: REST, HTTP (cheaper), WebSocket
Throttling, caching, usage plans, API keys
Lambda, HTTP, VPC Link integration targets
Canary deployments and access logging
Foundation for most serverless APIs on AWS

Route 53.explanation: AWS Route 53 is a scalable DNS service with health checking and traffic routing
points: Domain registration, DNS routing, health checks
Latency-based, geolocation, weighted, failover routing policies
Alias records for AWS resources (no extra charge)
Traffic flow visual editor for complex routing
Used by Netflix, Airbnb, many high-traffic sites

CloudWatch.explanation: CloudWatch collects logs, metrics, and alarms for all AWS resources in one place
points: Metrics, logs, events, alarms, dashboards, Synthetics
Container Insights and Lambda Insights
Application Insights for automatic problem detection
CloudWatch Logs Insights for powerful querying
Essential for monitoring and observability on AWS

CloudTrail.explanation: CloudTrail logs every API call made in your AWS account for auditing and compliance
points: Logs management events and data events
Multi-region trails and organization trails
Integration with CloudWatch Logs and EventBridge
Lake option for long-term storage and analytics
Critical for security auditing and compliance

Secrets Manager AWS.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager stores, rotates, and manages database passwords and API keys
points: Automatic rotation for RDS, Redshift, Aurora
Fine-grained IAM access control
Replication across regions for DR
Lambda-based custom rotation support
Eliminates hard-coded credentials in code

KMS.explanation: AWS Key Management Service creates and controls encryption keys for protecting data
points: Customer Master Keys (CMKs) — customer or AWS-managed
Envelope encryption pattern for large data
Automatic key rotation for customer-managed keys
Cross-account key sharing and multi-region keys
Integrated with most AWS services

WAF.explanation: AWS WAF filters malicious web traffic to protect your applications from attacks
points: Web ACLs with managed rules (AWS Managed Rules, third-party)
Rate-based rules for DDoS protection
Geo-restriction and IP allow/block lists
Integration with CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway
Fraud Control for account takeover prevention

Shield.explanation: AWS Shield provides automatic DDoS protection for all AWS resources
points: Standard protection free for all AWS customers
Shield Advanced adds 24/7 DDoS Response Team and cost protection
Layer 3/4 protection always on
Layer 7 protection via integration with WAF
Automatic detection and mitigation

GuardDuty.explanation: GuardDuty uses ML to continuously monitor AWS accounts for malicious activity
points: Analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs
Detects reconnaissance, instance compromise, credential abuse
Findings prioritized by severity
Automated response via EventBridge
Multi-account support through organizations

Regions.explanation: Cloud regions are geographic areas with multiple isolated data centers for redundancy
points: Each region is isolated from others for fault tolerance
Compliance and data residency requirements often dictate region choice
New services often launch in us-east-1 first
Inter-region latency typically 50–200 ms
Replication across regions required for global applications

Availability Zones.explanation: Availability Zones are isolated data centers within a region for high availability
points: Each AZ has independent power, cooling, networking
Minimum 2–6 AZs per region
Multi-AZ deployments provide automatic failover
Synchronous replication possible within region
Critical for achieving high availability SLAs

Edge Locations.explanation: Edge locations are CDN points of presence around the world that cache content close to users
points: Over 400 edge locations globally (CloudFront)
Reduce latency and origin load
Also run Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions
DDoS mitigation occurs at edge
Essential for global content delivery performance

Spot Instances.explanation: Spot instances are spare cloud capacity offered at up to 90% discount for interruptible workloads
points: Ideal for batch jobs, big data, CI/CD, stateless workloads
Spot Fleet and Spot Fleet Requests for diversification
Defined-duration Spot blocks for predictable time
Hibernation support for stateful workloads
Savings Plans can now apply to Spot usage

Reserved Instances.explanation: Reserved instances commit to 1 or 3 years of cloud usage for significant cost savings
points: Standard, Convertible, Scheduled RI types
All Upfront, Partial Upfront, No Upfront payment options
Convertible RIs allow changing instance type/family
Significant savings for predictable steady-state workloads
Being supplemented by Savings Plans for more flexibility

Savings Plans.explanation: AWS Savings Plans offer flexible discounts for consistent cloud compute usage
points: Compute Savings Plans — most flexible, applies to EC2, Fargate, Lambda
EC2 Instance Savings Plans — specific instance family commitment
Up to 72% savings vs On-Demand
1-year and 3-year terms
Recommended as primary discount mechanism (2025)

Cloud Cost Management.explanation: Cloud cost management uses tools and practices to control and optimize cloud spending
points: Tagging strategy is foundation of cost allocation
AWS Cost Explorer, Budgets, Cost Anomaly Detection
Third-party tools: CloudHealth, Cloudability, Harness
FinOps cultural practice gaining widespread adoption
Right-sizing, reserved capacity, spot usage are primary levers

FinOps.explanation: FinOps is the practice of bringing financial accountability to variable cloud spending
points: Three phases: Inform → Optimize → Operate
Cross-functional collaboration between engineering, finance, leadership
Focus on unit economics and business value of cloud spend
FinOps Foundation standards and certification program
Becoming table stakes for large cloud deployments

Shared Responsibility Model.explanation: Shared responsibility defines what the cloud provider secures versus what customers secure
points: Provider responsible for security *of* the cloud (hardware, facilities)
Customer responsible for security *in* the cloud (data, configs, IAM)
Varies by service type: IaaS → most customer responsibility
SaaS → most provider responsibility
Critical concept for compliance and security planning

Cloud Native.explanation: Cloud-native apps are designed from the ground up to use cloud services and scale elastically
points: CNCF definition includes containers, microservices, immutability, declarative APIs
Built with Kubernetes, service mesh, observability stack
Designed for automation, resilience, elasticity
12-factor principles still relevant
Goal is to maximize cloud benefits vs lift-and-shift

Twelve-Factor App.explanation: The Twelve-Factor methodology defines best practices for building scalable cloud-native apps
points: Codebase — one codebase tracked in revision control
Dependencies — declare and isolate
Config — store in environment
Backing services — treat as attached resources
Processes — execute as stateless processes
